title: Introduction to Derivatives
content: A derivative measures how a function changes as its input changes. For a function f(x), the derivative f'(x) gives the instantaneous rate of change at each point. Geometrically, it represents the slope of the tangent line to the graph of f at x. The derivative is defined as the limit of the difference quotient (f(x+h) - f(x)) / h as h approaches zero. Derivatives are a foundational tool in calculus with wide applications in physics, economics, and engineering.
subject: math

title: Chain Rule in Calculus
content: The chain rule allows us to differentiate composite functions. If y = f(g(x)), then dy/dx = f'(g(x)) * g'(x). In words, we take the derivative of the outer function evaluated at the inner function, times the derivative of the inner function. The chain rule is essential for handling expressions like (3x + 1)^5 or sin(x^2), where a naive application of basic rules would not work. Mastering the chain rule is a prerequisite for multivariable calculus.
subject: math

title: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
content: Given a square matrix A, a non-zero vector v is an eigenvector of A if Av = lambda*v for some scalar lambda, called the eigenvalue. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors reveal invariant directions of a linear transformation: directions along which the transformation acts purely as scaling. They are central to principal component analysis, stability analysis of dynamical systems, and the spectral theorem. Computing them typically involves solving the characteristic polynomial det(A - lambda*I) = 0.

title: The Scientific Method
content: The scientific method is a systematic process for investigating phenomena and acquiring new knowledge. It typically involves making observations, formulating a hypothesis, designing and conducting experiments to test the hypothesis, analyzing results, and drawing conclusions. A key requirement is that hypotheses must be falsifiable -- it must be possible, in principle, to gather evidence that would disprove them. Peer review and replication of experiments are critical to the integrity of scientific knowledge.
subject: biology

title: Cell Structure and Organelles
content: Eukaryotic cells contain membrane-bound organelles that perform specialized functions. The nucleus houses the genetic material. Mitochondria generate ATP through cellular respiration. The endoplasmic reticulum synthesizes proteins (rough ER) and lipids (smooth ER). The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts, and packages proteins for transport. Lysosomes digest cellular waste. Ribosomes, which can be free in the cytoplasm or attached to the rough ER, are responsible for protein synthesis. Understanding organelles is foundational to cell biology.
subject: biology

title: DNA Replication
content: DNA replication is the biological process by which a cell duplicates its genome before dividing. It is semiconservative: each daughter molecule contains one original strand and one newly synthesized strand. The process begins at origins of replication, where the double helix is unwound by helicase. DNA polymerase adds new nucleotides in the 5' to 3' direction, producing a leading strand continuously and a lagging strand in short Okazaki fragments. DNA ligase joins the fragments. Fidelity is maintained by proofreading and mismatch repair.
subject: biology

title: The Krebs Cycle
content: The citric acid cycle, also known as the Krebs cycle, is a series of chemical reactions used by all aerobic organisms to release stored energy. It takes place in the mitochondrial matrix and begins with acetyl-CoA combining with oxaloacetate to form citrate. Through eight enzyme-catalyzed steps, citrate is progressively oxidized, producing NADH, FADH2, ATP (or GTP), and CO2, and regenerating oxaloacetate. The reduced cofactors then feed electrons into the electron transport chain, driving oxidative phosphorylation.
subject: biology

title: The Fall of the Roman Empire
content: The fall of the Western Roman Empire is conventionally dated to 476 CE, when the last emperor Romulus Augustulus was deposed by the Germanic chieftain Odoacer. Historians debate the causes, but commonly cited factors include political instability, economic decline, over-reliance on mercenary armies, pressure from migrating peoples (the so-called 'barbarian invasions'), and the administrative strain of governing such a vast territory. The Eastern Roman Empire, centered on Constantinople, continued for nearly another thousand years as the Byzantine Empire.
subject: history

title: Causes of the French Revolution
content: The French Revolution (1789-1799) was the product of multiple converging pressures: a fiscal crisis worsened by France's support of the American Revolution, a rigid social hierarchy that placed enormous tax burdens on the Third Estate while exempting the clergy and nobility, Enlightenment ideas challenging the legitimacy of absolute monarchy, and a sequence of poor harvests that drove food prices up. The Estates-General of 1789, the storming of the Bastille, and the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen mark its critical early moments.
subject: history

title: Bretton Woods and the Postwar Economic Order
content: The Bretton Woods Conference of 1944 established the postwar international monetary system. Delegates from 44 Allied nations created the International Monetary Fund and what would become the World Bank, and agreed to a system of fixed exchange rates with the US dollar convertible to gold at USD 35 per ounce. This arrangement underwrote two decades of global economic stability but collapsed in 1971 when the United States unilaterally suspended dollar-gold convertibility, marking the transition to the modern system of floating currencies.

title: Variables and Data Types in Python
content: In Python, a variable is a name bound to a value. Python is dynamically typed, so variables do not have explicit type declarations -- the type is inferred from the value. Core built-in types include int, float, bool, str, list, tuple, dict, and set. Lists and dicts are mutable; tuples and strings are immutable. You can inspect a value's type with type(x) and check membership in a collection with the 'in' operator. Understanding mutability is crucial for avoiding subtle bugs when passing objects between functions.
subject: programming

title: List Comprehensions vs. Loops
content: A list comprehension is a concise way to build a list by iterating over an iterable, optionally filtering items. [x*x for x in range(10) if x % 2 == 0] produces the squares of even numbers from 0 to 8. Compared to a for-loop with append, list comprehensions are generally faster (the interpreter optimizes them) and read as a single expression, but they can become unreadable if nested too deeply or combined with side effects. A good rule: use a comprehension when the logic fits on one line without sacrificing clarity.
subject: programming

title: Asynchronous Programming with asyncio
content: Python's asyncio library provides a single-threaded concurrency model based on coroutines. You declare a coroutine with 'async def' and await other coroutines inside it. An event loop schedules coroutines cooperatively -- when one awaits I/O, the loop runs another. asyncio shines for I/O-bound workloads (HTTP requests, database calls) where threads would waste memory. It is not a fit for CPU-bound work, which still needs multiprocessing. Common primitives include asyncio.gather (run many coroutines concurrently) and asyncio.Semaphore (limit concurrency).
subject: programming

title: Type Hints and Static Analysis in Python
content: Type hints let you annotate variables, function arguments, and return values with expected types, e.g. def greet(name: str) -> str. They are not enforced at runtime -- Python remains dynamic -- but they enable tooling: IDE completions, safer refactoring, and static checkers like mypy that flag type errors before code runs. Modern Python supports rich types like list[int], dict[str, Any], Union (or '|' syntax), Optional, Literal, and Protocols for structural typing. Typed code is one of the most effective tools for scaling a codebase.
subject: programming

title: Database Indexes and B-trees
content: An index is a data structure that a database maintains alongside a table to speed up lookups. The most common index type is a B-tree (or its variant, the B+tree): a balanced tree where each node holds many keys, allowing O(log n) lookups with few disk pages read. Indexes make WHERE, JOIN, and ORDER BY clauses faster but cost space and slow down writes. Composite indexes cover multi-column queries, and covering indexes can satisfy a query without touching the table. Choosing the right indexes requires reading the query plan with EXPLAIN.
subject: programming

title: Vector Embeddings and Semantic Search
content: A vector embedding is a dense numerical representation of text (or images, audio, etc.) produced by a machine learning model. Embeddings capture semantic meaning: similar inputs produce vectors that are close in high-dimensional space under metrics like cosine similarity or Euclidean distance. Semantic search indexes these vectors so that a query is converted to its own embedding and matched against the index to retrieve the most semantically similar items -- not just keyword matches. Vector databases and extensions like pgvector make this practical at scale.
subject: programming

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
content: Retrieval-Augmented Generation combines a retrieval step over a corpus of documents with a generative language model. When a user asks a question, the system first retrieves relevant passages (often via vector search), then prompts an LLM with the question and the retrieved passages as context, instructing it to answer using that context. RAG reduces hallucinations, allows the model to use information outside its training data, and makes it straightforward to cite sources. Quality hinges on retrieval precision and careful prompt design.
subject: programming

title: Plate Tectonics
content: The Earth's lithosphere is fragmented into large rigid plates that move over the partially molten asthenosphere beneath them. Plate boundaries come in three flavors: divergent (plates move apart, forming mid-ocean ridges and rift valleys), convergent (plates collide, producing mountain ranges or subduction zones), and transform (plates slide past each other, producing faults such as the San Andreas). Plate tectonics explains earthquakes, volcanism, the distribution of continents, and the formation of many mineral deposits.
subject: science

title: Newton's Laws of Motion
content: Newton's three laws of motion are foundational to classical mechanics. The first law (inertia) states that an object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion stays in motion at constant velocity, unless acted on by a net external force. The second law quantifies force as F = m*a: the net force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration. The third law states that for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. Together they describe how forces cause changes in motion and underpin everything from projectile motion to orbital mechanics.
subject: science

title: The Second Law of Thermodynamics
content: The second law of thermodynamics states that the entropy of an isolated system never decreases: natural processes proceed in the direction of increasing disorder. Equivalently, heat cannot spontaneously flow from a cold body to a hot body without external work. The second law sets fundamental limits on the efficiency of heat engines (Carnot's theorem) and provides the 'arrow of time' -- the thermodynamic asymmetry between past and future. It has deep consequences in cosmology, chemistry, and information theory, where entropy measures the amount of uncertainty in a system.
